Les refroidissements fréquents ou infections grippales ( autres que la grippe ) sont des infections virales des voies respiratoires supérieures. Les symptômes typiques sont le rhume , une inflammation de la gorge / des muqueuses, une toux , associés à des maux de tête et de la fièvre. Les refroidissements surviennent généralement à la fin de l’automne, en hiver et au printemps. Boire beaucoup (thé, lait au miel , etc.) fait partie des recommandations pour atténuer les symptômes, au même titre que le rinçage nasal et les gargarismes . Symptômes Abattement (fatigue, manque de tonus) Fièvre , frissons Rhume / nez qui coule Maux de gorge , enrouement Gonflement des ganglions lymphatiques du cou

Toux , éternuements Maux de tête et douleurs dans les membres Durée: 7 à 10 jours Complications Infection bactérienne supplémentaire («surinfection») Bronchite Sinusite Otite Infection pulmonaire Toux de croup (chez les enfants) Causes et traitement Cause Infection virale par gouttelettes (en parlant, en éternuant, en toussant) Défenses immunitaires affaiblies par le manque de sommeil, le stress, des pièces surchauffées, une maladie préexistante Suivi au cabinet médical / à l’hôpital Examens possibles Examen physique (généralement suffisant) Traitements possibles Médicaments pour faire baisser la fièvre et soulager les douleurs (paracétamol, ibuprofène)

Médicaments pour fluidifier les sécrétions Il n’est généralement pas judicieux de prendre des antibiotiques. Que puis-je faire moi-même? Se ménager, éventuellement se reposer au lit Se laver les mains régulièrement Jeter ses mouchoirs en papier directement après utilisation Eternuer et tousser dans son coude Boire beaucoup (eau, jus de fruits, thé) Sprays décongestionnant pour le nez (max. 5 jours) Bains de bouche et de gorge désinfectants Remèdes maison Solution saline: pour le rinçage nasal et les gargarismes Lait au miel Tisane de sauge , tisane à la camomille , etc.

Renforcer son système immunitaire: dormir suffisamment, éviter le stress, prendre éventuellement des substances contenant de l’échinacée (effets controversés) Utiliser les huiles essentielles et le miel avec précaution chez les jeunes enfants ( allergie , détresse respiratoire ) Quand consulter un médecin? Fièvre élevée Intensification des douleurs (oreilles, visage, tête , thorax, dos ) Toux contenant du sang Difficultés respiratoires, détresse respiratoire Raideur dans la nuque, troubles de la conscience Symptômes au-delà de 10 jours Synonymes rhume, infection grippale, état grippal Spécialistes médicaux En savoir plus sur la personne Donnez votre avis sur l'article

PMC Copyright notice PMCID: PMC7129248 PMID: 29447989 Abstract Objectives To describe the role of bacteria (including bacterial resistance), viruses (including those recently described) and mixed bacterial–viral infections in adults presenting to primary care with lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI). Methods In all, 3104 adults with LRTI were enrolled, of whom 141 (4.5%) had community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), and 2985 matched controls in a prospective study in 16 primary care networks in Europe, and followed patients up at 28–35 days. We detected Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae and assessed susceptibility, atypical bacteria and viruses. Results

A potential pathogen was detected in 1844 (59%) (in 350 (11%) bacterial pathogens only, in 1190 (38%) viral pathogens only, and in 304 (10%) both bacterial and viral pathogens). The most common bacterial pathogens isolated were S. pneumoniae (5.5% overall, 9.2% in CAP patients) and H. influenzae (5.4% overall, 14.2% in CAP patients). Less than 1% of S. pneumoniae were highly resistant to penicillin and 12.6% of H. influenzae were β-lactamase positive. The most common viral pathogens detected were human rhinovirus (20.1%), influenza viruses (9.9%), and human coronavirus (7.4%). Influenza virus, human parainfluenza viruses and human respiratory syncytial virus as well as human rhinovirus, human coronavirus and human metapneumovirus were detected significantly more frequently in LRTI patients than in controls.

Conclusions A bacterial pathogen is identified in approximately one in five adult patients with LRTI in primary care, and a viral pathogen in just under half, with mixed infections in one in ten. Penicillin-resistant pneumococci and β-lactamase-producing H. influenzae are uncommon. These new findings support a restrictive approach to antibiotic prescribing for LRTI and the use of first-line, narrow-spectrum agents in primary care. Keywords: Aetiology, Lower respiratory tract infection, Respiratory Introduction

Community-acquired lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) is one of the commonest reasons for consulting in primary care and accounts for considerable antibiotic use and health-care costs. It is neither feasible nor cost-efficient to identify microbial aetiology in most patients who present with LRTI in primary care because of sampling challenges, limited access diagnostics and the limited clinical utility of receiving a result after empirical treatment decision has been made [1] . Consequently, little is known about the aetiology of LRTI in everyday primary care. In addition, detecting pathogens in both symptomatic patients and contemporaneous controls to distinguish between asymptomatic carriage and the presence of agents causing symptoms has rarely been carried out. Nevertheless, despite limited knowledge of the proportion of patients that have an identifiable bacterial aetiology and the sensitivities of these pathogens, and evidence of limited or no clinical benefit from antibiotic treatment, more than half of patients presenting to primary care with LRTI/acute cough in Europe are prescribed antibiotics [2] , [3] , [4] . This contributes to the selection of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria [5] . Improved knowledge of likely pathogens (at the point of care) and the likely susceptibility of bacterial pathogens, could help to guide antibiotic prescribing decisions and so help contain unnecessary antibiotic use and antimicrobial resistance. Furthermore, such information could support public health policy on prevention of respiratory illness, including vaccination.

Our primary objective was to describe the viral and bacterial aetiology in adult patients presenting to primary care with LRTI and in those with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). Our secondary objectives were to describe the presence of resistance in bacterial infections and of mixed viral–bacterial infections. Materials and methods Study design and patients

The study was part of the European Union FP6 funded Network of Excellence GRACE (Genomics to combat Resistance against Antibiotics in Community-acquired LRTI in Europe Network of Excellence; www.grace-lrti.org ). We recruited patients between October 2007 and April 2010 in 16 primary care networks that had a track record of conducting research based in 11 European countries: Antwerp and Ghent (Belgium); Barcelona and Mataro (Spain); Bialystok, Lodz and Szczecin (Poland); Bratislava (Slovakia); Cardiff and Southampton (UK); Jesenice (Slovenia); Jönköping (Sweden); Milan (Italy); Nice (France); Rotenburg (Germany) and Utrecht (the Netherlands).

Inclusion criteria for patients were: age ≥18 years, with an acute or worsened cough (≤28 days duration) as the main symptom, or any clinical presentation considered to be caused by LRTI by the general practitioner (GP) and consulting for the first time for this illness episode. Patients with presumed cough of non-infective origin, antibiotic consumption in the previous month, and any serious condition associated with an immunocompromised condition were excluded. For each patient, we planned to include a control patient matched for age, maximum 5 years of difference, and gender, consulting at the GP office for any other reason than acute respiratory illness within the same 2-week period. The study was approved by the local ethics committees in all participating centres and by the competent authority in each country. Written informed consent was obtained from each patient and control participant before inclusion.

Sampling and measurements Symptomatic patients were assessed at first presentation (day 1) and between days 28 and 35. Chest radiographs were taken within 1 week after inclusion. CAP was considered present if the local radiologist reported lobar or bronchopneumonia; other diagnoses were categorized as ‘pneumonia absent’ [6] .

All recruiting GPs received standardized sampling material and a protocol with detailed instructions on the sampling of the patients. Within 24 h of first presentation and inclusion, serum and EDTA blood, sputum, if available, and two nasopharyngeal flocked swabs (NPS; COPAN) were taken. At days 28–35, serum sampling and the two NPS were repeated. Controls were sampled for EDTA blood and two NPS at baseline. Sputum was not obtained from controls and the controls were not followed up. Serum, EDTA and NPS were stored frozen in the local laboratories until regular shipment to the central laboratory (University Hospital Antwerp), where specimens were stored at −80°C until analysis.
Bacterial cultures for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae

Sputum samples were examined in the local laboratories using direct microscopy to assess the quality (ratio of white blood cells/epithelial cells ≥1 as criterion for good quality), then Gram-stained, cultured and subsequently frozen at −80°C. Streptococcus pneumoniae and H. influenzae were identified using conventional biochemical tests and isolates were frozen in microbanks until shipped in batches to the central laboratory, where NPS were cultured for S. pneumoniae and/or H. influenzae . Their susceptibility was tested at the Karolinska Institute and the Oxford University, respectively, after frozen transport. The MICs of S. pneumoniae to penicillin G, erythromycin, clindamycin, tetracycline and levofloxacin were determined. Isolates were classified as sensitive, indeterminate or resistant according to the EUCAST breakpoints for these species ( www.eucast.org/antimicrobial-susceptibility-testing/breakpoints ). Haemophilus influenzae isolates were tested for β-lactamase production.

PCRs for Mycoplasma pneumoniae , Chlamydia pneumoniae , Bordetella pertussis , Legionella pneumophila and respiratory viruses Nucleic acid from NPS was extracted with the NucliSens EasyMag (bioMérieux, Marcy l'Étoile, France) in Antwerp after which aliquots were shipped to three collaborating laboratories for subsequent analysis with their in-house amplification and detection methods, which had been evaluated previously [7] . Serology for M. pneumoniae , C. pneumoniae and B. pertussis

For the detection of M. pneumoniae -specific and C. pneumoniae specific IgG or IgM antibodies, M. pneumoniae or C. pneumoniae IgG and IgM-ELISA kits (Medac GmbH, Wedel, Germany) were used according to the instructions of the manufacturer. IgG antibodies to B. pertussis toxin (Institut Virion-Serion GmbH, Würzburg, Germany) were analysed in a convalescent serum sample. Diagnostic criteria

The isolation of S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae , and the identification of L. pneumophila or respiratory viruses by use of PCR in respiratory samples were considered to support an aetiological diagnosis. Infection with M. pneumoniae or C. pneumoniae was defined as: positive PCR in respiratory samples, the presence of IgM antibodies in the acute-phase serum and/or convalescent-phase sample, IgG seroconversion or a significant increase in IgG between acute and convalescent samples.

A patient was considered positive for an acute B. pertussis infection (infection in the last 6 months) if positive by PCR in a respiratory sample and/or the presence of an antibody titre to pertussis toxin of ≥125 IU/mL in convalescent serum (days 28–35), demonstrated previously as a cut-off with high sensitivity and specificity [8] , [9] . Statistical analysis

Generalized estimating equations were used to assess differences in the proportion of potential pathogens between LRTI patients' day 1 and days 28–35 samples, and between day 1 samples of LRTI patients and controls. The case–control design was applied to assess causality between viral pathogens and LRTI (CAP). Chi-squared tests were used to assess differences in the proportion of specific viruses or bacteria between LRTI patients with and those without CAP. Student's t -test was used to assess differences in age between LRTI patients with and those without specific viral or bacterial aetiology (IBM ® SPSS ® Statistics, Release 20.0.0). A p value of <0.05 was considered to be statistically significant.

Twenty-four of 172 (14.0%) had a reduced susceptibility to penicillin G (one isolate highly resistant, 23 (13.4%) intermediate resistance). Thirty-six (20.9%) isolates were less susceptible to erythromycin/clindamycin, 78 (45.3%) had a reduced susceptibility to tetracycline and 3 (1,7%) were resistant to levofloxacin. Twenty-one of 167 (12.6%) H. influenzae isolates produced β-lactamases. Viral aetiology

Any viral aetiology was identified in 1494 (48.1%) of LRTI patients, significantly less often in those with CAP compared with those without CAP ( Fig. 1 and Table 2 , Table 3 ). The commonest viruses in our cohort of patients were human rhinovirus (HRV), influenza virus and human coronavirus (HCoV). A respiratory virus was detected on days 28–35 in 336 patients (12.6%), as well as in 205 (9.9%) of the matched controls. All respiratory viruses, except for human adenovirus, human bocavirus (HBoV) and WU polyomavirus and KI polyomavirus, were significantly more frequently detected in day 1 NPS of LRTI patients than in their days 28–35 NPS or in the NPS of their matched controls ( Table 3 ). Apart from human adenovirus, virus prevalence did not differ significantly between patients with CAP or with LRTI.

Among all 3104 LRTI patients, a mixed bacterial, mixed viral or mixed bacterial–viral infection was detected in 51 (1.6%), 118 (3.8%) and 304 (9.8%) patients, respectively. The pathogens involved are described in more detail in the Supplementary material . Discussion

This is the only prospective, large international, case–control study using standardized sampling and comprehensive microbiological work up to provide accurate estimates of the prevalence of both bacterial and viral aetiology in patients consulting with LRTI in primary care. The overall microbiological yield was high, mainly due to the high prevalence of viruses. A potential bacterial pathogen was isolated in only one in five patients, and antibiotic-resistant pathogens were rare. Comparison with literature

Previous studies have mainly studied more severely ill patients hospitalized with CAP rather than LRTI in primary care [1] , [10] , [11] , [12] , and few of those studies used comprehensive diagnostic methods, including PCR, to detect respiratory viruses [10] , [12] , [13] . We identified a potential pathogen in about 60% of CAP patients. However, comparisons are difficult in that our study is unique in terms of study design, the broad inclusion criteria, the high numbers of patients sampled at baseline and follow up, the inclusion of matched controls, and the comprehensive conventional and molecular microbiological diagnostics used. Bacterial aetiology and resistance in CAP

The prevalence of S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae in our CAP subgroup was significantly higher than in the non-CAP patients, but lower in comparison to most previous studies. We do not consider that the implementation of pneumococcal vaccine influenced our findings because of the small number of CAP patients who had been vaccinated. However, only 5% of patients in the most comprehensive aetiological study of adult patients hospitalized with CAP in the USA had pneumococcal pneumonia [14] . High-level penicillin resistance in pneumococci remains very low in all European countries in this setting, which supports the recommendation that if antibiotics are to be prescribed, amoxicillin should be the first-line agent for LRTI [1] . Mycoplasma pneumoniae infections occur in epidemics every 4–5 years: we included patients in our study between two epidemic waves, possibly explaining the low M. pneumoniae prevalence observed [15] , [16] . This is also the first large European prospective study on the prevalence of pertussis in adults consulting primary care physicians for acute cough [17] .

Importance of respiratory viruses, including newly detected viruses We detected at least one respiratory viral pathogen in almost 50% of patients. NPS sampling may have yielded significantly more infected respiratory epithelial cells [18] , with sensitive PCR-based diagnostic techniques augmenting specifically for viruses. Influenza virus, human parainfluenza viruses 1–4 and respiratory syncytial virus are recognized causes of CAP in hospitalized patients and in the elderly [13] Influenza vaccination resulted in lower prevalence of influenza virus in the elderly (data not shown). HRV, HCoV and HMPV are rarely detected in CAP and other LRTI in outpatients.

HRV has been associated with outbreaks of severe respiratory disease, including CAP, in older people [19] , [20] , [21] and has been isolated in hospitalized patients with CAP [10] , but a prevalence of 14.2% in CAP in outpatients is high and a novel finding. HCoV have recently been identified in small numbers of adults with severe pneumonia [10] , [21] , but is not routinely tested for in adult outpatients with CAP or LRTI. We may have underestimated the prevalence of HCoV as HKU-1 testing was not performed and HKU-1 is generally as prevalent as NL63 and OC43 [22] . Infections due to HMPV are mainly described in long-term care facilities [10] . We found HMPV more prevalent in outpatients with CAP compared with those with other LRTIs, with even greater prevalence in CAP patients than respiratory syncytial virus, and similar to the 3%–7% HMPV infection prevalence found in hospitalized adults [23] . Although numbers are small, human adenovirus was significantly more prevalent in CAP compared with other LRTI, a unique finding in immunocompetent outpatients. The high rates of viral detection in outpatients with LRTI and CAP suggests that comprehensive microbiological assessment is important to guide management and may explain the limited average benefit from antibiotic treatment in the placebo-controlled study that we conducted in a large subset of patients included in the present analysis [2] .

Our study is the first that compared the prevalence of respiratory viruses in symptomatic adults with that in matched controls without respiratory symptoms. Influenza virus, human parainfluenza viruses 1–4 and respiratory syncytial virus were never, or rarely, detected in controls or at follow up in symptomatic patients. This strongly implicates these agents as causative pathogens. Similarly, the significantly lower prevalence of HRV, HMPV and HCoV in patients at follow up and in controls suggests that asymptomatic carriage of these viruses is uncommon in adults, and indicates that these viruses should also be regarded as causative agents in CAP [11] , [14] , [23] .
For HRV, the rates of prolonged shedding (same genotype in 35%) versus re-infection (other genotype) in the GRACE study have been further investigated [24] .

Human bocavirus was detected in CAP and in <1% of LRTI patients at baseline, with similar findings among controls and at follow up of patients. HBoV was identified in respiratory specimens from 1.5% of hospitalized adults with no alternative viral aetiology, but controls were not included in that study [25] . As HBoV is often found in the presence of other pathogens in respiratory specimens we agree that HBoV probably has no relevance or primary role as a causative agent in LRTI in primary care [26] . There may be an association between high HBoV viral loads and HBoV being the only virus detected [27] , suggesting that a quantitative approach should be considered [26] .

This also applies to KI polyomavirus and WU polyomavirus. Although it is not yet possible to draw firm conclusions on their role in human pathology [28] , [29] , [30] , our data show no evidence for a causative role in outpatient CAP or LRTI—assessment of the viral loads could potentially help to further clarify their significance. Limitations

Sputum was not obtained from all patients, and sputa and follow-up serology were not obtained from control patients. Consequently, a valid estimation of the prevalence of bacterial pathogens in controls was not always possible. Although the most important elements of this study are the descriptive results, we also performed multiple statistical tests so the finding of statistical significance may reflect type I error. However this is much less likely when supporting prior work on aetiology (e.g. bacterial causes of CAP) or when the p-value is very small (e.g. the case–control comparisons of viral aetiology). Conclusions and implications for future management of LRTI

This unique comprehensive prospective study using modern microbiological methods suggests that the traditional view of aetiology in CAP and outpatient LRTI should be revised. We have found that viral CAP and LRTI are also caused by HRV, HCoV and HMPV. Our high viral detection rates should also inform clinical decision making. Better diagnostics are needed to distinguish viral from bacterial CAP or LRTI at the point of care.

The current study provides microbiological evidence for why antibiotics do not help patients with LRTI. Only approximately one in five LRTI patients have a bacterial pathogen isolated and so could conceivably benefit from antibiotic treatment. This evidence should support primary care clinicians' restrictive approach to antibiotic prescribing for LRTI. If they consider antibiotics are indeed indicated, the low resistance levels in S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae should support the prescription of narrow-spectrum antibiotics. BACKGROUND: Influenza is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality, particularly in critically ill patients. The availability of effective antiviral therapies is pivotal in mitigating the severity and complications associated with influenza. OBJECTIVES: This review evaluates the antivirals available for the treatment of severe influenza in critically ill patients, focusing on the strength of recommendations and levels of evidence derived from clinical trials, observational studies, and guidelines. The aim is to provide clinicians with evidence-based insights to optimize antiviral strategies in the intensive care unit setting.

SOURCES: A comprehensive literature search was conducted using PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases for studies published up to January 2025. Keywords included "antiviral therapy," "influenza," "critically ill patients," "oseltamivir," "peramivir," "zanamivir," "lanimavir," "baloxavir," and "favipiravir." Additional references were identified from the bibliographies of relevant articles. CONTENT: The following topics are covered: antivirals available for treating influenza and evidence supporting their use in critically ill patients, pharmacokinetic issues of enteral oseltamivir administration in critically ill patients, and neuraminidase inhibitors resistance.

IMPLICATIONS: Neuraminidase inhibitors constitute the vast majority of antivirals currently prescribed for influenza. The most commonly prescribed neuraminidase inhibitor to date is oseltamivir. Although its efficacy in nonsevere cases of influenza is well established, the evidence for its efficacy in critically ill patients is based on less robust studies, as no randomized controlled trials have been conducted in this population. Limited data on oseltamivir pharmacokinetics is available in critically ill patients. The selection of A(H1N1)pdm09 resistant variants to oseltamivir is particularly problematic in critically ill patients hospitalized in intensive care units.

Data on other antivirals, such as neuraminidase inhibitors (i.e. zanamivir, peramivir and laninamivir) or baloxavir marboxil in critically ill patients are scarce. Further research is needed to develop new drugs and assess their efficacy in critically ill patients and to better assess the effect of oseltamivir in this population. Copyright © 2025 The Author(s). BACKGROUND: Antiviral post-exposure prophylaxis with neuraminidase inhibitors can reduce the incidence of influenza and the risk of symptomatic influenza, but the efficacy of the other classes of antiviral remains unclear. To support an update of WHO influenza guidelines, this systematic review and network meta-analysis evaluated antiviral drugs for post-exposure prophylaxis of influenza. METHODS: We systematically searched MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature,

Global Health, Epistemonikos, and ClinicalTrials.gov for randomised controlled trials published up to Sept 20, 2023 that evaluated the efficacy and safety of antivirals compared with another antiviral or placebo or standard care for prevention of influenza. Pairs of reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. We performed network meta-analyses with frequentist random effects model and assessed the certainty of evidence using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) approach. The outcomes of interest were symptomatic or asymptomatic infection, admission to hospital, all-cause mortality, adverse events related to antivirals, and serious adverse events. This study is registered with PROSPERO, CRD42023466450.

FINDINGS: Of 11 845 records identified by our search, 33 trials of six antivirals (zanamivir, oseltamivir, laninamivir, baloxavir, amantadine, and rimantadine) that enrolled 19 096 individuals (mean age 6·75-81·15 years) were included in this systematic review and network meta-analysis. Most of the studies were rated as having a low risk of bias. Zanamivir, oseltamivir, laninamivir, and baloxavir probably achieve important reductions in symptomatic influenza in individuals at high risk of severe disease (zanamivir: risk ratio 0·35, 95% CI 0·25-0·50; oseltamivir: 0·40, 0·26-0·62; laninamivir: 0·43,

0·30-0·63; baloxavir: 0·43, 0·23-0·79; moderate certainty) when given promptly (eg, within 48 h) after exposure to seasonal influenza. These antivirals probably do not achieve important reductions in symptomatic influenza in individuals at low risk of severe disease when given promptly after exposure to seasonal influenza (moderate certainty). Zanamivir, oseltamivir, laninamivir, and baloxavir might achieve important reductions in symptomatic zoonotic influenza in individuals exposed to novel influenza A viruses associated with severe disease in infected humans when given promptly after exposure (low certainty). Oseltamivir, laninamivir, baloxavir, and amantadine probably decrease the risk of all influenza (symptomatic and asymptomatic infection; moderate certainty). Zanamivir, oseltamivir, laninamivir, and baloxavir probably have little or no effect on prevention of asymptomatic influenza virus infection or all-cause mortality (high or moderate certainty). Oseltamivir probably has little or no effect on admission to hospital (moderate certainty). All six antivirals do not significantly increase the incidence of drug-related adverse events or serious adverse events, although the certainty of evidence varies.

INTERPRETATION: Post-exposure prophylaxis with zanamivir, oseltamivir, laninamivir, or baloxavir probably decreases the risk of symptomatic seasonal influenza in individuals at high risk for severe disease after exposure to seasonal influenza viruses. Post-exposure prophylaxis with zanamivir, oseltamivir, laninamivir, or baloxavir might reduce the risk of symptomatic zoonotic influenza after exposure to novel influenza A viruses associated with severe disease in infected humans. OBJECTIVES: For many decades, guaifenesin and dextromethorphan have been two of the most well-established and commonly used nonprescription medications to manage cough and cold symptoms. A single source that summarizes the clinical data supporting the use of guaifenesin and dextromethorphan as self-care treatment options in cough and cold could assist healthcare professionals (HCPs) in making informed recommendations to patients. The objective of this narrative review is to discuss the benefits of guaifenesin and dextromethorphan for the management of cough and mucus-related cold symptoms in adults by examining published data on the effectiveness and safety of the products containing these ingredients.

METHODS: Literature searches were performed on PubMed, Embase, and MEDLINE to identify randomized, controlled studies comparing guaifenesin or dextromethorphan treatment with placebo control in adults with cough and cold (mucus) symptoms. Of 36 guaifenesin and 53 dextromethorphan clinical studies initially identified by the literature search, 13 guaifenesin and 19 dextromethorphan publications met the predefined inclusion criteria. Additional studies were identified during manuscript development by reviewing the citations of included articles, for a total of 17 guaifenesin and 21 dextromethorphan publications.

RESULTS: Data from studies of guaifenesin and dextromethorphan either used alone or combined with other active ingredients showed statistically significant improvements compared with placebo control in sputum looseness/adhesiveness and reductions in cough frequency/severity, respectively. A small number of studies did not show significant improvements with study drug compared with placebo control. Conflicting data may originate from differences in study design, patient enrollment, and a relatively high placebo control effect across studies.

CONCLUSION: The data reviewed in this article support the importance of guaifenesin and dextromethorphan in the armamentarium of effective nonprescription treatment options for cough and mucus-related cold symptoms. DOI: 10.1080/00325481.2025.2603034 PMID: 41423743 [Indexed for MEDLINE]

Human metapneumovirus (hMPV) is a significant cause of respiratory infections worldwide, particularly in young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals. Since its discovery in 2001, hMPV has been recognized as a major contributor to acute respiratory tract infections, along with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and influenza. This review explores the virology, epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, diagnostic methods, and recent advances in therapeutic and preventive strategies for hMPV infection. By consolidating current knowledge, we aim to highlight the importance of hMPV in public health and the need for continued research to address its clinical and economic burdens.

Introduction Human metapneumovirus (hMPV), a member of the Pneumoviridae family, was first identified in the Netherlands in 2001 from respiratory samples collected over a 20-year period. Its discovery filled a significant gap in our understanding of respiratory pathogens, as many cases of acute respiratory tract infections remain unattributed to known viruses. hMPV is closely related to Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), sharing structural and genetic similarities, and is now recognized as one of the leading causes of respiratory infections worldwide [ 1 ].

The virus primarily targets the respiratory epithelium, causing infections that range from mild upper respiratory symptoms to severe lower respiratory tract illnesses, such as bronchiolitis and pneumonia [ 1 – 3 ]. While it affects individuals across all age groups, its impact is particularly severe in young children, the elderly, and those with compromised immune systems. Studies estimate that nearly all children are exposed to hMPV by the age of five, highlighting its pervasive nature [ 1 , 4 , 5 ]. In adults, especially those with underlying conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or asthma, hMPV can exacerbate pre-existing respiratory issues, leading to significant morbidity and healthcare utilization [ 6 – 8 ].

hMPV exhibits a seasonal pattern of circulation, with peaks typically occurring during late winter and early spring in temperate regions [ 9 , 10 ]. This seasonality overlaps with that of other respiratory viruses, complicating clinical diagnosis and public health management [ 11 ]. Despite its clinical importance, hMPV remains underdiagnosed because its symptoms are often indistinguishable from those caused by RSV, influenza, or other respiratory pathogens.

From a public health perspective, hMPV poses a considerable burden, contributing to hospitalizations, outpatient visits, and economic costs associated with respiratory disease [ 12 ]. Advances in molecular diagnostics have improved detection rates; however, many cases remain unrecognized, underscoring the need for greater awareness and diagnostic capacity. Furthermore, the absence of specific antiviral treatments and licensed vaccines for hMPV emphasizes the critical need for research focused on therapeutic and preventive measures against hMPV.

The subsequent sections of this review delve into the virology, epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnostic methods, and current state of therapeutic and vaccine development for hMPV. By synthesizing existing knowledge, we aim to provide a comprehensive overview of this significant respiratory pathogen and identify key areas for future research. Virology

HMPV is an enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA virus with a genome of approximately 13 kb in length; however, the genome size of RSV is approximately 15 kb and that of the Influenza Virus is 13.5 kb (Table 1 ). The genome is organized into 10 genes encoding nine proteins, including nucleoprotein (N), phosphoprotein (P), matrix protein (M), fusion protein (F), glycoprotein (G), small hydrophobic protein (SH), large polymerase protein (L), and two non-structural proteins (M2-1 and M2-2) (Fig. 1 A-B). The viral structure consists of an RNA-protein complex surrounded by a lipid envelope embedded with F, G, and SH surface proteins. These proteins play pivotal roles in the viral life cycle, host interactions, and immune evasion [ 13 , 14 ].

Open in a new tab The F protein is responsible for the fusion of the viral envelope with the host cell membrane, facilitating its entry. It is highly conserved across hMPV strains and serves as a critical target for vaccine and antiviral drug development. The G protein mediates attachment to host cells, although it is less conserved than the F protein. The M protein assists in the assembly of virions. The SH protein, while less well understood, is believed to contribute to immune evasion by modulating host responses [ 1 , 15 , 16 ].

hMPV is divided into two major genetic lineages, A and B, each further subdivided into sublineages A1, A2, B1, and B2. These genetic variations influence the antigenic properties of the virus but do not significantly affect clinical presentation [ 17 , 18 ]. They primarily affect G proteins, leading to antigenic diversity and complicating immune responses. Despite this diversity, the F protein remains relatively stable, making it an ideal target for therapeutic interventions [ 17 – 19 ].

Replication of hMPV occurs in the cytoplasm of host cells and involves the formation of viral replication complexes. The virus employs a negative-sense RNA genome that must first be transcribed into a positive-sense RNA template by the viral polymerase before protein synthesis can occur [ 20 ]. hMPV also encodes non-structural proteins that regulate the host immune response, such as the inhibition of type I interferon signaling, allowing the virus to evade early immune detection [ 21 , 22 ]. Phosphorylation of the M2-1 protein has been found in vivo to be essential for viral replication and pathogenesis of viral infections, and it is possible that inhibition of M2-1 phosphorylation may be important for the development of vaccines as well as antiviral drugs for pneumoviruses [ 23 ].

Studies using animal models and cell cultures have revealed that hMPV has a broad tropism for respiratory epithelial cells and can induce significant cytopathic effects, including syncytium formation [ 3 ]. The ability to form multinucleated giant cells is a hallmark of hMPV and contributes to tissue damage and inflammation during infection [ 24 ]. Recent advances in structural virology have provided detailed insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying hMPV entry and replication, paving the way for rational drug design. Epidemiology

hMPV circulates worldwide and affects populations across diverse geographic and climatic regions. Seasonal peaks are observed in temperate areas during late winter and early spring, coinciding with the circulation of other respiratory viruses such as influenza and RSV. This overlap often complicates clinical diagnosis and epidemiological research. In tropical regions, hMPV circulation is less defined but in recorded epidemic periods, it has been observed that cases often peaked during the rainy seasons [ 25 ]suggesting an environmental influence on transmission dynamics [ 9 – 11 , 25 , 26 ].

hMPV is a leading cause of bronchiolitis, pneumonia, and exacerbations of asthma and COPD [ 6 ]. Infants under two years of age are particularly vulnerable, with nearly universal exposure to the virus by the age of five [ 1 , 4 , 5 ]. Hospitalization rates for hMPV-related lower respiratory tract infections in children rival those of RSV, underscoring its clinical significance [ 27 , 28 ]. In addition to children, older adults and immunocompromised individuals face a heightened risk of severe disease, prolonged viral shedding, and complications such as secondary bacterial infections [ 4 ].

Recent seroprevalence studies have indicated that hMPV infections contribute significantly to the global burden of respiratory diseases [ 29 ]. Co-infection with RSV, influenza, or bacterial pathogens may complicate diagnosis and treatment [ 30 ]. Epidemiological data suggest that hMPV accounts for 5–15% of hospitalizations for acute respiratory illnesses, with higher rates in pediatric and geriatric populations. Surveillance efforts have revealed that outbreaks can occur in community settings, long-term care facilities, and hospitals, highlighting their transmissibility and public health impact [ 31 , 32 ].

The virus primarily spreads through respiratory droplets and direct contact with contaminated surfaces. Household transmission is common, with asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic individuals often serving as reservoirs for the spread of the disease. A recent study that performed regression models at the individual and household levels showed that hMPV transmission was positively associated with the age of the index case, the increase of which was directly related to the probability of human metapneumovirus transmission within households [ 33 ]. This poses challenges for infection control, particularly in healthcare and communal living environments [ 34 , 35 ]. The lack of routine testing for hMPV further complicates surveillance and outbreak management, emphasizing the need for improved diagnostic capability.

Advances in molecular diagnostics, such as multiplex PCR platforms, have enhanced the ability to detect hMPV and differentiate it from other respiratory pathogens [ 36 ]. However, underreporting remains an issue, particularly in resource-limited settings, where access to these technologies is restricted. Ongoing global surveillance and epidemiological studies are essential to better understand the virus’s transmission patterns, risk factors, and public health impact. Pathogenesis of human metapneumovirus infections

Pathogenesis of hMPV infections is characterized by the virus’s ability to target and infect the respiratory epithelium, leading to a cascade of cellular damage, inflammation, and immune activation [ 2 , 15 , 37 ]. Upon inhalation, hMPV primarily infects the epithelial cells lining the upper and lower respiratory tracts. The virus uses its F and G proteins to facilitate viral attachment and fusion with host cell membranes, initiating the replication process. Although it has been shown that in most paramyxoviruses, the attachment of the F and G proteins is essential for binding and infection, the role of the G protein in receptor binding in hMPV infections has not been elucidated, in contrast to its role in RSV infections, indicating a primary role of the F protein [ 16 ]. Viral replication and assembly occur in the cytoplasm, with newly formed virions released to infect neighboring cells, amplifying the infection [ 20 , 38 ].

Epithelial cell infection triggers the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, such as IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-8, which recruit immune cells to the site of infection. Neutrophils, macrophages, and lymphocytes infiltrate respiratory tissues, contributing to inflammation and tissue damage [ 15 , 39 ] (Fig. 2 ). Studies have shown that this immune-mediated response plays a dual role: while it is essential for viral clearance, excessive inflammation can lead to immunopathology, exacerbating disease severity [ 40 , 41 ]. Recognition of Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV) by Pattern Recognition Receptors and Modulation of Interferon Response. HMPV is detected by various receptors, and its ability to modulate the interferon (IFN) response is influenced by viral proteins. Pattern recognition receptors in the lower respiratory tract, such as RIG-I and MDA-5, detect HMPV replication through two primary pathways. The first pathway relies on RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs), including RIG-I and MDA-5. These receptors initiate signaling through interactions with MAVS, resulting in the release of type I interferons (IFNs). Additionally, pro-inflammatory cytokines and type III IFNs are produced via the activation of IRF3 and NF-κB, respectively. RLRs are activated by viral replication products, such as cytosolic double-stranded RNAs (dsRNAs) and uncapped 5′-triphosphates found in genomic RNA [ 41 , 115 ]. The second pathway involves Toll-like receptors (TLRs), specifically TLR3, TLR4, and TLR7, which recognize viral proteins. Activation of TLR3 (in most cells) and TLR7 triggers type I IFN secretion via the TIR domain-containing adaptor-inducing IFN-β (TRIF)/IRF3-dependent and MyD88/IRF7-dependent pathways, respectively [ 116 ]. However, the G protein of HMPV impairs TLR4 signaling. HMPV proteins play a significant role in the inhibition of viral recognition. The G and P proteins (in HMPV strain B1) prevent the detection of viral RNA by blocking the RIG-I- and MAVS-dependent signaling pathways. Additionally, the M2-2 and SH proteins are critical virulence factors that suppress signaling through both pathways [ 41 ]. The image was created using BioRender.com hMPV employs several mechanisms to evade host immune response. The innate immune system serves as the first line of defence against hMPV infection. Pattern recognition receptors, including Toll-like receptors and RIG-I-like receptors, detect viral RNA and trigger downstream signaling pathways (Fig. 2 ). This leads to the production of type I and III interferons, which inhibit viral replication and recruit immune cells to the site of infection. However, hMPV can antagonize the interferon response through viral proteins, such as M2-2, which suppresses IFN production [ 21 , 42 ]. The virus interferes with type I interferon signaling, a critical component of the innate immune response, by inhibiting the activation of interferon regulatory factors (IRFs) and the downstream production of antiviral interferons [ 21 , 22 ]. This allows the virus to replicate efficiently in the early stages of infection. Additionally, hMPV modulates adaptive immune responses by impairing dendritic cell function, leading to suboptimal T cell activation and delayed viral clearance [ 37 , 43 ]. However, hMPV infection does not confer long-lasting immunity, leading to the possibility of reinfections [ 44 ].

Animal models and in vitro studies have demonstrated that hMPV infection results in significant histopathological changes, including epithelial cell detachment, loss of ciliary function, and formation of syncytia, multinucleated giant cells formed by the fusion of infected cells. These changes disrupt mucociliary clearance, a critical defense mechanism of the respiratory tract, and predispose individuals to secondary bacterial infections [ 24 ]. hMPV-induced tissue damage results from direct viral cytopathology, as viral replication can cause epithelial cell apoptosis and necrosis. In contrast, immune-mediated damage to host tissues due to neutrophilic inflammation and overproduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines could be a consequence of excessive immune responses during hMPV infection [ 45 – 47 ].

In severe cases, particularly in immunocompromised individuals and those with underlying respiratory conditions, hMPV infection can extend beyond the epithelial layer, causing alveolar damage, pulmonary edema and impaired gas exchange. This can lead to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), a life-threatening complication [ 48 ]. Understanding the molecular and immunological mechanisms underlying hMPV pathogenesis is crucial for developing effective therapeutic and preventive strategies against hMPV infections. Targeting viral proteins involved in immune evasion and modulating the host immune response to prevent excessive inflammation represents a promising avenue for future research.

Clinical manifestations hMPV infection presents a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations, ranging from mild upper respiratory tract illness to severe lower respiratory tract disease [ 2 ]. In most cases, hMPV infection results in symptoms that overlap significantly with those of other respiratory viruses such as RSV and influenza. Typical symptoms include rhinorrhea, cough, sore throat, and fever. These symptoms are often self-limiting in healthy individuals but can escalate in severity depending on age, immune status, and comorbidities [ 2 , 49 ].

In children, hMPV is a leading cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia. It is particularly prevalent in infants and young children under two years of age, who often present with wheezing, increased respiratory effort, and hypoxemia [ 32 , 50 ]. Other common hMPV manifestations in children include laryngotracheobronchitis (croup) and acute otitis media [ 51 ]. Studies have shown that hMPV infection can exacerbate pre-existing conditions, such as asthma, contributing to acute asthma attacks and hospitalizations. Additionally, co-infection with other respiratory pathogens, including RSV, influenza, and bacterial agents, is common and can worsen disease outcomes [ 32 , 52 ].

In adults, the clinical presentation of hMPV varies widely from mild to severe. While many cases are mild and resemble a common cold, older adults and those with underlying conditions such as COPD or congestive heart failure are at greater risk of severe disease. Symptomatic hMPV infection is more common in individuals > 65 years of age, and symptoms in this population often include shortness of breath, cough, fever, and chest pain [ 53 ]. In severe cases, hMPV can lead to acute respiratory failure, requiring hospitalization and intensive care unit (ICU) admission [ 4 , 6 – 8 , 35 ]. In a prospective study, 18% of adult patients with hMPV infection experienced a complicated disease course, with nearly a third of them requiring ICU admission and ventilatory support, whereas death occurred in 8.3% of all patients, highlighting the importance of hMPV as a respiratory pathogen [ 54 ].

Immunocompromised individuals, including transplant recipients and patients undergoing chemotherapy, are particularly vulnerable to prolonged and severe hMPV infection. These patients may experience atypical manifestations such as persistent fever, extensive lung involvement, and secondary bacterial infections. Moreover, as noted in a recent meta-analysis of viral infections in lung transplant recipients, hMPV infection is a significant cause of chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD), with a pooled 1-year incident of 32% in these patients [ 55 ]. Prolonged viral shedding in immunocompromised populations increases the risk of nosocomial transmission, further complicating infection control [ 56 , 57 ].

Complications of hMPV infection include secondary bacterial infections, such as otitis media, sinusitis, and bacterial pneumonia, which are particularly common in pediatric and elderly populations [ 58 – 60 ]. Rarely, severe cases may progress to ARDS, necessitating mechanical ventilation and leading to significant morbidity and mortality [ 48 ]. Understanding the full clinical spectrum of hMPV infection is critical for improving its diagnosis and management. Early recognition, particularly in high-risk populations, can help mitigate severe outcomes and reduce the overall disease burden. Diagnosis

Early diagnosis of hMPV infection, given that there are currently no effective vaccines or specific antiviral agents against hMPV, would significantly assist in the timely care of patients and the containment of its outbreak [ 61 ]. The diagnosis of hMPV infections relies on advanced laboratory techniques to accurately detect the virus and differentiate it from other respiratory pathogens. The most reliable method is reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), which offers high sensitivity and specificity. RT-PCR can identify hMPV-specific RNA sequences in respiratory specimens, such as nasopharyngeal swabs, sputum, and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, and has become the gold standard for hMPV detection [ 62 , 63 ]. The advent of multiplex PCR platforms has further enhanced diagnostic capabilities by allowing the simultaneous detection of multiple respiratory pathogens, including hMPV, RSV, and influenza [ 64 , 65 ].

In addition to RT-PCR, immunofluorescence assays (IFAs) are used to identify hMPV antigens in respiratory samples. Although IFAs are less sensitive than molecular methods, they remain valuable in clinical laboratories where RT-PCR may not be readily available [ 66 , 67 ]. Serological tests that detect specific antibodies against hMPV are less commonly employed due to their retrospective nature and delayed antigen response following acute infection [ 1 , 68 ].

Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) is a highly sensitive and efficient isothermal amplification method that facilitates rapid pathogen detection, including hMPV, at approximately 65 °C with minimal equipment. For instance, Song et al. designed RT-LAMP assays targeting the M gene, achieving limits of detection (LOD) of 4.33 and 3.53 copies/µL for hMPV genotypes A and B, respectively, making it ten times more sensitive than conventional RT-PCR [ 69 , 70 ]. Similarly, Wang et al. developed RT-LAMP assays targeting the N gene, with an LOD of < 10 copies/µL, highlighting their potential for field applications with visual readouts [ 71 ].

Recombinase-Aided Amplification (RAA) offers another rapid, simple technique, operating at 39 °C and delivering results within 15 minutes [ 72 ]. Jiao et al. developed an RT-RAA assay for the hMPV N gene with an LOD of 100 copies/µL, demonstrating its efficiency compared to traditional RT-qPCR [ 73 ]. Furthermore, metagenomic Next-Generation Sequencing (mNGS) provides a high-throughput method for identifying known and novel pathogens, including hMPV, as demonstrated by Xu et al., who identified hMPV in 80% of the tested samples using nanopore sequencing, although its routine clinical use is limited by cost and complexity [ 74 , 75 ]. In addition, mNGS can be used to amplify the entire hMPV genome with high accuracy [ 72 ].

Finally, virus isolation remains the gold standard for pathogen diagnosis, offering insights into viral biology and vaccine development, despite being labor-intensive and time-consuming, and relying on cell lines such as LLC-MK2 and CRFK to confirm hMPV antigens or nucleic acids after incubation [ 36 , 76 ].

Advancements in point-of-care (POC) testing are emerging, offering rapid diagnostic solutions for the detection of hMPV. These tests are designed to provide results within minutes to hours and are particularly useful in outpatient and emergency settings. However, their sensitivity and specificity are generally lower than those of laboratory-based methods, warranting confirmation in cases of high clinical suspicion [ 77 , 78 ].

Future directions in hMPV diagnostics include the development of highly sensitive and specific rapid tests and novel technologies, such as CRISPR-based diagnostics, which offer the potential for on-site and low-cost testing [ 78 ]. The CRISPR-Cas12a system is considered a powerful tool for the in vitro detection of nucleic acids [ 79 ]. Qian et al. developed a technique for detecting hMPV RNA by combining RT-RPA with the CRISPR-Cas12a system. RT-RPA combined with the Cas12a-based LF assay is a rapid detection method that does not require specialized equipment and shows a detection agreement of 96.4% with quantitative RT-PCR analysis [ 56 ].

Accurate diagnosis of hMPV infection is crucial for guiding clinical management and implementing public health interventions. Misdiagnosis or delayed identification can lead to inappropriate use of antibiotics, increased healthcare costs, and a heightened risk of nosocomial transmission. Standardized protocols for sample collection, processing, and interpretation of results are essential to ensure the reliability of diagnostic outcomes [ 80 ].

Despite these advances, several challenges remain in the diagnosis of hMPV infections (or detection of hMPV). Limited access to molecular diagnostics in resource-constrained settings contributes to underreporting and gaps in the surveillance data. Additionally, the overlapping clinical presentations of hMPV with other respiratory viruses highlight the need for integrated diagnostic approaches that combine clinical, epidemiological, and laboratory findings [ 81 , 82 ]. Enhanced diagnostic tools will play a pivotal role in improving the recognition and management of hMPV, ultimately reducing its burden on the healthcare system. Therapeutic strategies

Therapeutic options for hMPV remain limited, and no specific antiviral agents are currently approved for clinical use. The management of hMPV infections is largely supportive, focusing on alleviating symptoms and preventing complications. Supportive care includes oxygen therapy for hypoxemia, intravenous fluids for dehydration, and mechanical ventilation in severe cases of respiratory failure. Early recognition and intervention are critical for improving outcomes in high-risk patients. Antiviral agents

Although no antivirals are specifically licensed for hMPV, several agents have shown promise in preclinical and early-stage clinical studies. Ribavirin, a broad-spectrum antiviral drug, has demonstrated efficacy against hMPV in vitro and in animal models [ 83 ]. However, its clinical use is limited by toxicity concerns and inconsistent results in human studies [ 84 , 85 ]. Similarly, nucleoside analogs and small-molecule inhibitors targeting viral RNA polymerase or fusion proteins are under investigation [ 86 , 87 ].

Monoclonal antibodies targeting the hMPV F protein have emerged as promising therapeutic agents. Preclinical studies have shown that these antibodies can neutralize the virus and reduce disease severity [ 88 , 89 ]. Palivizumab, an RSV-targeted monoclonal antibody, has shown cross-reactivity with hMPV and may offer partial protection [ 90 , 91 ]. Efforts to develop monoclonal antibodies specifically against hMPV are ongoing, with several candidates undergoing preclinical and early phase clinical trials.

Furthermore, oligopeptides derived from the viral F protein have also been used as viral fusion inhibitors, with promising results in mouse models of hMPV infection, and the NMSO3 sialyl lipid has been shown to reduce viral replication and ameliorate lung inflammation in BALB/c mice [ 92 , 93 ]. Broad-spectrum antivirals

Broad-spectrum antivirals, such as remdesivir, initially developed for other viral infections such as Ebola and COVID-19, have shown potential activity against hMPV in laboratory studies [ 94 , 95 ]. These agents target viral replication and may provide a therapeutic option for severe cases or co-infections involving multiple respiratory viruses [ 94 , 95 ]. Further clinical trials are needed to evaluate the safety and efficacy of these drugs against hMPV infections. Host-Directed therapies

Given hMPV’s ability to evade immune responses and induce excessive inflammation, host-directed therapies offer a novel approach for managing infection [ 43 , 96 ]. Immunomodulators, such as corticosteroids and cytokine inhibitors, may help mitigate immunopathology in severe cases [ 97 ]. Additionally, therapies aimed at enhancing innate immune responses, such as interferon-based treatments, are being investigated. Adjunctive therapies

Adjunctive therapies, including antioxidants and agents targeting oxidative stress pathways, are being explored to reduce lung injury and improve outcomes in severe hMPV infections [ 98 – 100 ]. Supportive pharmacological interventions, such as bronchodilators, may provide symptomatic relief in patients with airway obstruction or reactive airway disease [ 101 , 102 ]. Challenges and future directions

The development of effective therapies for hMPV faces several challenges, including limited funding, difficulties in conducting large-scale clinical trials, and a lack of robust animal models that fully replicate human disease. Collaborative efforts between academia, industry, and government agencies are essential to accelerate research and development in this field.

Future strategies should focus on identifying novel antiviral targets, optimizing monoclonal antibody therapies, and exploring combination treatments that address both viral replication and host immune responses. The integration of precision medicine approaches, leveraging genomic and proteomic data, may enhance therapeutic efficacy and reduce adverse effects. Preventive measures Efforts to develop vaccines and preventive strategies for hMPV are gaining momentum, with several promising candidates currently in preclinical and clinical trials. The primary focus has been on targeting the highly conserved F protein, which plays a crucial role in viral entry and fusion with host cells.
Vaccine development

Numerous vaccine platforms are under development, including live-attenuated, subunit, and vector-based vaccines. Live-attenuated vaccines aim to mimic natural infections, stimulating robust immune responses while maintaining safety in vulnerable populations, such as young children and the elderly [ 103 ]. Subunit vaccines, which use purified viral proteins such as the F protein, focus on eliciting neutralizing antibodies with minimal risk of adverse effects [ 104 ]. Vector-based vaccines, which employ viral vectors to deliver hMPV antigens, represent a versatile approach capable of inducing both humoral and cellular immunity [ 105 – 107 ]. Several vaccine candidates have demonstrated efficacy in preclinical animal models, and early phase human trials have yielded encouraging results.

Monoclonal antibodies for passive immunization Monoclonal antibodies targeting the F protein offer another promising preventive strategy, especially for high-risk populations such as immunocompromised individuals, infants, and the elderly. Palivizumab, originally developed for RSV, has shown limited cross-reactivity with hMPV [ 88 – 91 ]. Newer monoclonal antibodies specifically engineered for hMPV are under development and have shown potent neutralizing activity in vitro and in vivo [ 108 , 109 ]. These antibodies may provide passive immunity during peak hMPV seasons or in outbreak scenarios. Non-Pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs)

Non-pharmaceutical interventions remain vital in reducing the spread of hMPV, particularly in the absence of licensed vaccines or antivirals. Measures such as frequent handwashing, use of alcohol-based hand sanitizers, respiratory etiquette (e.g., covering coughs and sneezes), and avoiding close contact with infected individuals are effective in breaking transmission chains [ 110 , 111 ]. Environmental disinfection of high-touch surfaces in healthcare and communal settings plays a crucial role in mitigating nosocomial transmission [ 112 , 113 ]. Community and healthcare setting strategies

Enhanced surveillance and rapid diagnostic testing are essential for the early identification of hMPV outbreaks, enabling the timely implementation of containment measures. In healthcare settings, protective measures such as the isolation of infected patients, use of personal protective equipment (PPE), and rigorous infection control protocols are critical. Public health campaigns can raise awareness of hMPV and promote preventive behaviors during seasonal peaks. Conclusion and future directions

hMPV represents a critical public health challenge because of its significant impact on global morbidity, mortality, and economic costs associated with respiratory illnesses. Despite substantial advances in understanding its biology, epidemiology, and clinical manifestations, several gaps remain in the development of effective therapeutic and preventive measures for this disease.

The lack of licensed antiviral drugs and vaccines for hMPV underscores the urgent need for further research and innovation. Advances in molecular virology and immunology have identified key viral components, such as the F protein, as promising targets for both therapeutic and vaccine development. However, the antigenic diversity of hMPV, particularly in the G protein, and the incomplete immune responses following natural infection present challenges in creating broadly protective and durable interventions [ 114 ].

Diagnostics have seen significant progress with the introduction of molecular techniques, such as RT-PCR and multiplex PCR platforms, enabling rapid and accurate detection of hMPV. However, disparities in access to diagnostic tools, particularly in resource-limited settings, contribute to underreporting and hinder global surveillance. Future developments should focus on affordable point-of-care diagnostics to improve case detection and outbreak management.

Current therapeutic strategies are limited to supportive care, with experimental agents such as monoclonal antibodies and broad-spectrum antivirals showing promise in preclinical and early phase clinical trials. Research into host-directed therapies and combination treatments targeting both viral replication and immune modulation could further enhance patient outcomes, especially in high-risk populations, such as young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals.

Preventive measures, including non-pharmaceutical interventions, remain the cornerstone of hMPV management in the absence of vaccines and specific therapies. Continued efforts to develop and integrate hMPV vaccines into routine immunization schedules for respiratory pathogens, such as RSV and influenza, could significantly reduce the disease burden. Multivalent vaccines targeting multiple respiratory viruses are particularly promising for enhancing vaccination compliance and cost-effectiveness.

Future directions in hMPV research should focus on several critical areas to enhance vaccination compliance and cost effectiveness. Comprehensive studies are needed to better understand the mechanisms of pathogenesis and immune evasion, which are fundamental for developing targeted therapeutic and preventive strategies. Efforts should prioritize the accelerated development and clinical evaluation of novel antivirals, vaccines, and monoclonal antibodies to address the current lack of specific treatment options. Expanding global surveillance networks is essential for monitoring hMPV epidemiology, tracking strain variations, and responding effectively to outbreaks. Additionally, the integration of emerging technologies, such as CRISPR-based diagnostics and precision medicine approaches, can significantly improve the accuracy of disease detection and treatment. Finally, strengthening public health education and awareness campaigns will play a pivotal role in enhancing the recognition, prevention, and management of hMPV infections, ultimately reducing its global impact.

Addressing these priorities will require interdisciplinary collaboration among researchers, clinicians, industry stakeholders and policymakers. By bridging the gaps in knowledge and infrastructure, the global health community can reduce the clinical and economic burdens of hMPV and improve outcomes for affected populations.
